question: In an interview with ‘Der Standard’ on 22 September 2025, Michael Schmid, President of the EU Agency for Criminal Justice Cooperation (Eurojust), stated that the EU had now overtaken the USA as the world’s largest market for cocaine. Mr Schmid added that cases registered with Eurojust has surged by 60% over the past five years, with drugs worth a total of around EUR 20 billion seized.

Most of the narcotics are transported from South America to Europe by container ship, but criminal networks are responding to more stringent checks in large ports by establishing new import routes and increasingly switching to smaller ports 1.

These alarming findings by Eurojust, revealing as they do a veritable explosion in drugrelated crime in Europe, are an indictment of the Commission's security policy and raise questions about possible links with the wave of mass illegal immigration since 2015. 1.

What specific measures does the Commission plan to take to meaningfully combat the proliferation of cocaine in Europe and protect the European population from the growing risks of international drug crime?
How does the Commission explain the dramatic 60% surge in cases registered by Eurojust and the seizure of drugs worth a total of around EUR 20 billion?
Does the Commission acknowledge any links between the massive increase in drugrelated crime in Europe in recent years and mass illegal immigration since 2015?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.1.2026) The European Drug Report 20251 points to high availability of cocaine in the EU. As announced in ProtectEU2, the Commission adopted an EU action plan against drug trafficking3 and a new EU drugs strategy4 in 2025.

The strategy seeks to address the drug situation in a balanced, comprehensive approach; the action plan will promote targeted activities addressing drug trafficking routes, enhancing crime prevention and international cooperation. In 2026, the Commission will propose new rules on organised crime to dismantle criminal networks more effectively.

The Commission encourages Member States to transpose as a matter of priority the 2024 asset recovery and confiscation rules should be transposed to strengthen the follow the money approach5. Moreover, through the European Ports Alliance and upcoming Ports Strategy, the Commission is reinforcing public-private security cooperation across all ports.

Half of the EU’s most dangerous criminal networks are involved in drug trafficking6, which is and will remain a key threat to internal security7. The new action plan against drug trafficking aims to strengthen law enforcement and judicial cooperation efforts.

The Commission has started negotiations to increase Eurojust operational cooperation with key third countries through cooperation agreements, notably with Latin America. There is no evidence highlighting a specific link between migration and cocaine trafficking in Europe.

1 https://www.euda.europa.eu/publications/european-drug-report/2025_en. 2 COM(2025) 148 final. 3 COM(2025) 744 final. 4 COM(2025) 743 final. 5 Directive (EU) 2024/1260 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 April 2024 on asset recovery

and confiscation, OJ L, 2024/1260, 2 May 2024. 6 Europol (2024), Decoding the EU’s most threatening criminal networks. 7 Europol (2025), EU Serious and Organised Crime Threat Assessment, https://www.europol.europa.eu/cms/sites/default/files/documents/EU-SOCTA-2025.pdf.
